newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Belgian hi-tech home looking for buyers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Belgian hi-tech home looking for buyers.

text.p: Want to fill your bath by remote control? Tango to your virtual radio?
Enter the 21st century with a Belgian home full of the latest comforts and conveniences modern technology can offer.
The price? For $5 million the House of the Future on the northeastern edge of Brussels can be yours.
Opened in 1995 as a showcase for what is possible in the appliance of science and technology in the home, it offers a glimpse of how our future lives could be transformed.

"A few people are interested in buying it, though nobody has made an offer yet," Frank Belien of the architectural firm which built it in 1995 told Reuters. The money raised from visits will go towards building a successor in just over three years' time.
"A buyer could pay $5 million today, but we would rent the house back until March, 2000 for $1 million," Belien added.
For around 140 companies, including telecoms and software firms, waste recyclers and a landscape gardener the house is a chance to show off their wares.
The House of the Future looks functional and industrial from the outside. It is an asymmetrical amalgam of curves and corners, with the south-facing walls made of glass panels.

Its secret lies in a unique structure and its flexibility, Belien says. Because only four pillars and two concrete beams support the whole building, partitioning walls can be knocked through at a whim if the owner fancies re-designing the layout.
At its heart, in the living room, is a computerised "house keeper" which controls lighting and temperature -- automatically working the sunscreens, curtains and energy-saving heating.
On a screen the computer shows who is who ringing the door bell or visitors who called while you were out.
For music, crank up the "virtual" hifi -- a two-dimensional screen image which works like the real thing.
Everything can be operated remotely on your way home.

Online shopping from the kitchen saves a tiresome trip to the supermarket. Scan coded labels on your empty packages before you throw them out and let the computer re-order everyday provisions before the cupboards get bare.
It won't order toilet rolls, though, because the ecological lavatory is paperless, using water and hot air instead.
A super-speed cooker heats food with magnetic coils under iron pans, acting twice as fast as gas while the surface of the hob stays cold to the touch.
Upstairs the bed sits up with you in the morning while breakfast television descends from the ceiling.

The bathroom looks conventional enough, but turn on the shower and there is no water -- only steam and piped Madonna songs to lather to. No chance of the mirror fogging up either, as it is heated from behind.
Dusty blinds have been banished into history. Blast electricity through a window containing liquid crystals and it turns into frosted glass.

Belien does not think life in the "intelligent" house turns its inhabitants into couch-potatoes, whose only worry is deciding which video-on-demand to watch or what to buy in computer-generated shopping malls linked up via the Internet.
"You just increase the level of your comfort -- it gives you more time to do other things," he said.

More time to play, but also to work. The office down the hall is calling, with the latest software, video-conferencing facilities, and fax machines that can save 100,000 pages on compact discs. There is not a paper clip in sight.

One local resident showing more than a passing interest in the House of the Future is Belgium's Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene. His American wife Celie works part-time on the site as a public relations executive.
"We live nearby and my husband saw it being built. He was very interested," Celie Dehaene said in between entertaining a party of visitors.
"The older people in particular are interested as they spend a lot of time in their houses. There are things here which are good for mothers at home with children and for disabled people."
She had also picked up one or two new ideas for improving the Dehaenes' own house, and especially liked the newly developed durable paint used on the interior walls.
"I have ordered the visitor-viewing system for the door, and they are going to paint our hall like this. When you see how many visitors they have here, it's amazing the paintwork's not even damaged."
